content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the quota declaration and delete, the quota
107	read and remaining query, the price
108	declaration and price delete, the price read and the price change history, and the usage, bill, and
109	metrics queries. An empty
110	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
111	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
112	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
113	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
114	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
115	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
116	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
117	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
118	the usual `409 conflict`.
119	
120	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
121	hold:
122	
123	```http
124	PUT /quotas
125	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
126	X-Tenant-Id: acme
127	
128	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
129	```
130	
131	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
132	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer, and may additionally
133	carry the optional `growth` object described below; a non-positive,
134	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
135	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Every quota
136	route requires a tenant: declaring, deleting, and reading without
137	`X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an
138	unknown query parameter on the delete or the remaining query is rejected the
139	same way, with the message naming the offending parameter. The response is
140	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
141	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
142	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
143	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
144	
145	Besides the two limits a declaration may carry one optional `growth` object
146	naming an automatic expansion policy for each limited resource. A policy
147	names only the resources it covers, and a resource it omits is never raised
148	automatically. Each named resource must declare exactly a positive integer
149	`step` and a positive integer `cap`, and the cap must not be below the
150	resource's declared limit:
151	
152	```http
153	PUT /quotas
154	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-2
155	X-Tenant-Id: acme
156	
157	{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}
158	```
159	
160	A missing field, an unknown field (inside the policy or beside it), a
161	non-object policy, a resource other than `workflows` or `executions`, or a
162	step or cap that is non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite is a
163	`400 validation_error`; a cap below the resource's declared limit is rejected
164	the same way. Every such rejection writes nothing. A declaration without
165	`growth` is byte-for-byte the two-limit request above; repeating a declaration
166	replaces limits and policy as a whole, so a declaration that names no `growth`
167	also drops the tenant's previous policy. The declaration response and the
168	quota read include the policy only when one is declared, with each entry
169	listing `step` before `cap` and resources in workflows-first order:
170	
171	```json
172	{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}}
173	```
174	
175	```http
176	GET /quotas
177	X-Tenant-Id: acme
178	```
179	
180	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
181	when the tenant has declared none.
182	
183	A tenant can also remove the quota it declared, on the same path with the
184	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other quota writes:
185	
186	```http
187	DELETE /quotas
188	Idempotency-Key: quota-delete-1
189	X-Tenant-Id: acme
190	
191	{}
192	```
193	
194	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body, an
195	unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that touches
196	no quota. The delete removes the declaration as a whole and leaves no partial
197	write, so a later read gives the same definite empty result as for a tenant
198	that never declared one: the delete response and every following read both
199	return `{"quota":null}`, and the remaining query lists neither resource —
200	neither limit, holding, nor remaining — and repeats with exactly the same
201	result. Deleting the quota of a tenant that never declared one returns that
202	same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete clears only the
203	declaration: it deletes no existing workflow or execution, and data already
204	held stays fully usable. It writes no metering record, so recorded usage
205	counts and bill conclusions already reached stay exactly as they were; later
206	writes simply run without a quota check until the tenant declares again.
207	
208	The delete follows the same idempotency rules as every other write: the
209	`Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same delete with the same
210	key returns the first result and performs no second removal, and reusing a
211	key for another operation — including a quota declaration — in the same
212	tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's quota unchanged. Quotas
213	are scoped per tenant like everything else: deleting one tenant's quota never
214	affects another tenant's declaration or remaining room. A missing or empty
215	tenant and a missing idempotency key are `400 validation_error`, and every
216	failed validation writes nothing — no quota row, no metering record, and no
217	price-table change history.
218	
219	A separate read-only entry point reports how much room the declared quota
220	leaves, with the same calling shape as the quota read:
221	
222	```http
223	GET /quotas/status
224	X-Tenant-Id: acme
225	```
226	
227	Each limited resource gives three numbers — the declared `limit`, the
228	`held` count the quota decision itself uses, and the `remaining` room, which
229	is simply limit minus holding — in that key order, with workflows first and
230	executions second; the same query repeats with the same ordering:
231	
232	```json
233	{"status":{"workflows":{"limit":10,"held":3,"remaining":7},"executions":{"limit":100,"held":12,"remaining":88}}}
234	```
235	
236	Lowering a limit below the current holding reports the `remaining` room
237	truthfully as a negative number; it is neither clamped to zero nor rejected.
238	A tenant that has never declared a quota gets the definite empty result
239	`{"status":null}`, listing neither resource. The query is strictly read-only:
240	it writes no metering record and changes no declared quota, usage, bill,
241	scheduling, approval, or replay conclusion, and another tenant's quota and
242	holdings are never visible and never influence the result. It requires a
243	tenant and accepts no query parameters: a missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id`
244	header, an unknown parameter (named in the error message), or a repeated
245	parameter is a `400 validation_error`, and these rejections write nothing.
246	
247	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the write is admitted
248	once the resource declares a growth policy that can make room: the declared
249	limit is raised in whole steps — the smallest number of `step` increments
250	that admits the write — never past the `cap` and never by a partial final
251	step, and the raised limit commits with the write in the same transaction,
252	so the request succeeds instead of returning a conflict. The expansion
253	changes only the declared limit: it writes no metering record, changes no
254	recorded usage count, and changes no bill conclusion already reached.
255	Repeating the same write with the same idempotency key returns the first
256	result without a second expansion, and reusing that key for another
257	operation is the usual `409 conflict`. Without a policy on the resource, or
258	when no whole-step raise within the cap can admit the write — including when
259	the cap already leaves no room for one more holding — the whole request is
260	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
261	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
262	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
263	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write and leaves the limit
264	untouched: nothing is inserted and previously stored data is unaffected,
265	exactly as for validation failures. The quota read and the remaining query
266	report the raised limit; the remaining query's `remaining` room is computed
267	from it.
268	
269	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
270	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
271	is at its execution limit, a growth policy raises the limit exactly as for a
272	manual creation and the period fires normally; when there is no policy or
273	the cap leaves no room a whole step can reach, the due period creates no
274	execution and the schedule is left unchanged — its cursor,
275	`last_triggered_at`, and `last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the
276	period is settled on a later pass once capacity exists, under the usual
277	per-period idempotence. Delivery history follows the tenant of the execution
278	it belongs to.
279	
280	### Tenant price tables
281	
282	The bill's baseline unit prices are built in. A tenant may instead declare
283	its own price table on a separate entry point with the same calling shape as
284	the quota declaration:
285	
286	```http
287	PUT /prices
288	Idempotency-Key: price-request-1
289	X-Tenant-Id: acme
290	
291	{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}
292	```
293	
294	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must be a non-empty
295	JSON object giving a map of metered action type to a positive-integer unit
296	price in cents. A non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite price,
297	an unknown metered type, a missing field (an empty object), an extra field
298	that is not a metered type, or a non-object body is a `400
299	validation_error` that writes nothing. Every price route requires a tenant:
300	declaring, deleting, and reading without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
301	one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an unknown query parameter on the
302	read or the delete is rejected the same way, with the message naming the
303	offending parameter. The response is
304	`{"prices":{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}}`, with the
305	declared types in ascending type-identifier order.
306	
307	A successful declaration replaces the tenant's price table as a whole with
308	exactly the types given this time; metered types the declaration does not
309	name fall back to the built-in default prices when a bill is taken. The
310	declaration rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken
311	before it was made.
312	
313	```http
314	GET /prices
315	X-Tenant-Id: acme
316	```
317	
318	Returns the price table currently declared by the tenant, in ascending
319	type-identifier order, or the definite empty result `{"prices":null}` for a
320	tenant that has never declared one. The stored table lists only the types
321	the declaration named; types left at the default are not copied into it.
322	
323	A tenant can also remove the table it declared, on the same path with the
324	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other price writes:
325	
326	```http
327	DELETE /prices
328	Idempotency-Key: price-delete-1
329	X-Tenant-Id: acme
330	
331	{}
332	```
333	
334	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body,
335	an unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that
336	touches no price table. The delete removes the table as a whole and leaves
337	no partial write: it is atomic with the declaration and the read, so a
338	concurrent reader sees either the complete old table or no table at all.
339	After it succeeds the tenant no longer holds a declared table, and both the
340	delete response and the following read give the definite empty result
341	`{"prices":null}`. Deleting the table of a tenant that never declared one
342	returns that same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete
343	rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken before it was
344	made; afterward both the bill and the bucketed bill price every type at the
345	built-in default, each line still giving the metered type, the actual
346	`unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent `subtotal`.
347	
348	The declaration and the delete follow the same idempotency rules as every
349	other write: the `Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same
350	declaration or the same delete with the same key returns the first result
351	and performs no second replacement or removal, and reusing a key for
352	another operation — including another price declaration or a price delete
353	— in the same tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's price
354	table unchanged. Price tables are scoped per tenant like everything else: a
355	tenant can never read or delete another's declaration, and another tenant's
356	declaration or deletion never affects this tenant's bill amounts.
357	
358	The bill and the bucketed bill price with the price table in effect **at
359	query time**: a named type uses the tenant's declared price and every other
360	type uses the built-in default. Each returned line still gives the metered
361	type, the actual `unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent
362	`subtotal`, and the total is exactly the sum of the listed subtotals; types
363	with no matching record are still omitted rather than listed at zero. A
364	declaration affects only later queries — it neither rewrites recorded usage
365	nor revises historical bills — changes no metering, and leaves the bill and
366	usage queries read-only. A delete affects only later queries in the same
367	way: the table is removed as a whole, later bills fall back to the
368	built-in defaults, and recorded usage and already-taken bills stay exactly
369	as they were.
370	
371	### Price-table change history
372	
373	Every successful price-table declaration or delete leaves one change record,
374	so a caller can see exactly when each repricing and each table removal took
375	effect. A separate entry point returns the tenant's change history:
376	
377	```http
378	GET /prices/history?limit=50
379	X-Tenant-Id: acme
380	```
381	
382	Returns `{"history":[...]}` with the records in ascending order of occurrence
383	time; records sharing one instant are ordered by a stable ascending sequence.
384	Each record is:
385	
386	```json
387	{"sequence":7,"action":"declare","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z","snapshot":{"execution_started":200}}
388	```
389	
390	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant,
391	  shared across every kind of price change. It identifies the record across
392	  every query and is never renumbered by a filter or a page;
393	- `action` is `declare` for a price-table declaration or `delete` for a
394	  removal;
395	- `occurred_at` is the moment the change took effect, an ISO-8601 UTC string
396	  ending in `Z`;
397	- `snapshot` is the table in effect after the change. A declaration's
398	  snapshot is the type-to-unit-price map that took effect, listing only the
399	  types that declaration named and in ascending type-identifier order; a
400	  delete's snapshot is `null`.
401	
402	The history record is written atomically with the change it describes, in the
403	same transaction as the price-table write, so a reader always sees the table
404	and its history agree and a rejected declaration, delete, or idempotency-key
405	conflict leaves no record. Repeating an idempotent declaration or delete with
406	the same key returns the first result and appends no second record; reusing a
407	key for another operation is the usual `409 conflict` and, again, writes no
408	history. A delete of a table that was never declared still succeeds and still
409	leaves its own `delete` record (with a `null` snapshot), exactly as it returns
410	the definite empty result for the table itself.
411	
412	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
413	`{"history":[]}`, never an error. The response is one line of compact JSON
414	with the record keys in the order above, full number precision preserved, and
415	a single trailing newline, like every other JSON endpoint.
416	
417	The endpoint accepts an optional action filter, the same optional closed time
418	window the per-record usage query accepts, plus cursor pagination:
419	
420	```http
421	GET /prices/history?action=declare,delete&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
422	```
423	
424	- `action` names one action or a comma-separated set of them (`declare` and
425	  `delete`); only records whose action is in the set are returned. A single
426	  value needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
427	  action is a `400 validation_error`; when `action` is absent every change is
428	  returned;
429	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
430	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
431	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
432	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing
433	  and the definite empty list is returned;
434	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
435	  contains more than that many records;
436	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
437	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
438	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
439	- the action filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
440	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
441	
442	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `action` entry, a
443	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
444	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
445	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
446	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
447	appends no history, changes no price table, and changes no metering, usage,
448	bill, quota, or scheduling conclusion. History follows the usual tenant
449	isolation, so another tenant's changes are never visible under any action
450	filter, window, or page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and
451	recovery leave every recorded sequence, time, and snapshot unchanged.
452	
453	### Usage metering and billing
454	
455	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
456	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
457	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
458	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
459	metered action types are:
460	
461	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
462	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
463	  definition;
464	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
465	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
466	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
467	  `schedule_triggered`;
468	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
469	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
470	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
471	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
472	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
473	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
474	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
475	  meters nothing.
476	
477	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
478	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
479	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
480	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
481	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
482	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
483	
484	```http
485	GET /usage
486	X-Tenant-Id: acme
487	```
488	
489	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
490	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
491	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
492	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
493	
494	```http
495	GET /bill
496	X-Tenant-Id: acme
497	```
498	
499	Returns the per-type bill:
500	
501	```json
502	{"bill":{"items":[
503	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
504	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
505	],"total":2100}}
506	```
507	
508	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
509	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
510	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
511	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`. The price used per type is
512	the tenant's declared price when its price table names that type and the
513	built-in default otherwise, read from the table in effect at query time (see
514	[Tenant price tables](#tenant-price-tables)); tenants with no declaration are
515	billed byte for byte as before.
516	
517	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
518	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
519	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`, plus an optional fixed time
520	bucket:
521	
522	```http
523	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
524	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
525	X-Tenant-Id: acme
526	```
527	
528	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
529	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
530	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
531	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
532	  as before;
533	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
534	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
535	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
536	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
537	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
538	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
539	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
540	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
541	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
542	  `0`.
543	
544	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
545	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
546	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
547	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
548	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
549	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
550	
551	Both endpoints also accept an optional `bucket` parameter for a fixed-bucket
552	trend summary, so callers never have to pull records and group them
553	themselves:
554	
555	```http
556	GET /usage?bucket=hour&since=2026-09-26T00:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-27T00:00:00.000Z
557	GET /bill?bucket=day&type=execution_started
558	X-Tenant-Id: acme
559	```
560	
561	- `bucket` is exactly `hour` or `day`: `hour` buckets start on the UTC hour
562	  and `day` buckets at UTC midnight, both aligned solely to UTC. An empty or
563	  any other value is a `400 validation_error`, exactly like a repeated
564	  parameter or an unknown query parameter;
565	- when `bucket` is present, usage returns
566	  `{"usage_buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T08:00:00Z","usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}, ...]}`:
567	  the buckets with at least one matching record, in ascending bucket-start
568	  order. Each entry gives its `bucket_start` first — an ISO-8601 UTC string
569	  ending in `Z` at the hour or midnight — followed by `usage`, the per-type
570	  counts inside that bucket in ascending type-identifier order; a type with no
571	  record in the bucket is omitted;
572	- when `bucket` is present, the bill returns
573	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T00:00:00Z","items":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100}, ...],"subtotal":100}, ...],"total":100}}`.
574	  Buckets appear in ascending bucket-start order; each bucket's `items` stay
575	  sorted by ascending type identifier, each line giving the filtered count,
576	  the usual positive-integer `unit_price`, and an integer-cent `subtotal` of
577	  the two, and a type with no matching record is omitted rather than reported
578	  at zero. Each bucket also carries its own `subtotal`, and the window
579	  `total` is exactly the sum of the listed per-bucket subtotals, all amounts
580	  integer cents;
581	- a bucket that holds no matching record never appears, so an empty tenant, a
582	  window with `since` later than `until`, or a filter that matches nothing
583	  returns the definite empty bucket lists `{"usage_buckets":[]}` and
584	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[],"total":0}` — never an error, with the empty bill's
585	  total at `0`;
586	- bucketing applies together with the type filter and the time window as an
587	  intersection: a bucket holds only records whose occurrence time is in the
588	  closed window **and** whose type the filter names. The window keeps its
589	  closed endpoints, its open bounds when either side is omitted, and the
590	  existing rule for when a record's instant falls in it; buckets are simply
591	  the same matching records rolled up to their UTC bucket;
592	- the bucketed queries are read-only like the others: they append no usage
593	  records, change no metering basis or prices, and never alter recorded usage
594	  or billing conclusions — under event replay or recovery the same window,
595	  type filter, and bucket always give the same answer;
596	- omitting `bucket` leaves both queries exactly as before: the same compact
597	  JSON responses with `usage` / `items` shapes, full float precision and the
598	  `-0.0` convention, byte for byte. The parameter introduces no second
599	  protocol and changes no entry point's existing behavior.
600	
601	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
602	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
603	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
604	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
605	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
606	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
607	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
608	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
609	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
610	
611	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
612	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
613	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
614	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
615	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.
616	
617	### Per-record usage history
618	
619	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
620	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
621	checked against the moment it occurred:
622	
623	```http
624	GET /usage/records?limit=50
625	X-Tenant-Id: acme
626	```
627	
628	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
629	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
630	sequence. Each record is:
631	
632	```json
633	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
634	```
635	
636	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
637	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
638	  filter or a page;
639	- `type` is the metered action type;
640	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
641	  ending in `Z`.
642	
643	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
644	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
645	like every other JSON endpoint.
646	
647	The endpoint accepts an optional metered-type filter, the same optional
648	closed time window the events and usage queries accept, plus cursor
649	pagination:
650	
651	```http
652	GET /usage/records?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
653	```
654	
655	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them;
656	  only records whose type is in the set are returned. A single identifier
657	  needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered
658	  type is a `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is
659	  returned, exactly as before;
660	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
661	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
662	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
663	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
664	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
665	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
666	  contains more than that many records;
667	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
668	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
669	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
670	- the type filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
671	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
672	
673	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `type` entry, a
674	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
675	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
676	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
677	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
678	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
679	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
680	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
681	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every
682	recorded sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.

684	### Operational metrics
685	
686	```http
687	GET /metrics
688	X-Tenant-Id: acme
689	```
690	
691	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
692	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
693	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
694	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
695	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
696	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
697	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
698	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
699	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
700	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
701	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
702	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
703	
704	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
705	timestamp ending in `Z`:
706	
707	```http
708	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
709	X-Tenant-Id: acme
710	```
711	
712	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
713	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
714	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
715	  counts every recorded fact;
716	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
717	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
718	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
719	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
720	  result.
721	
722	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
723	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
724	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
725	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
726	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
727	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
728	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
729	completion or termination event.
730	
731	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
732	
733	```http
734	GET /metrics/export
735	X-Tenant-Id: acme
736	```
737	
738	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
739	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
740	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
741	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
742	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
743	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
744	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
745	
746	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
747	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
748	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
749	ordered by ascending label value:
750	
751	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
752	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
753	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
754	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
755	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
756	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
757	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
758	  unlabeled scalar samples.
759	
760	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
761	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
762	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
763	ends with a single newline.
764	
765	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
766	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
767	failures, and schedule triggers:
768	
769	```json
770	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
771	```
772	
773	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
774	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
775	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
776	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
777	  ended for that reason.
778	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
779	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
780	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
781	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
782	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
783	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
784	  another attempt, per node identifier.
785	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
786	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
787	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
788	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
789	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
790	
791	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
792	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
793	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
794	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
795	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
796	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
797	
798	### Health
799	
800	```http
801	GET /health
802	```
803	
804	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
805	
806	### Create a workflow
807	
808	```http
809	POST /workflows
810	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
811	
812	{
813	  "id": "order-flow",
814	  "nodes": [
815	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
816	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
817	  ]
818	}
819	```
820	
821	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
822	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
823	
824	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
825	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
826	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
827	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
828	
829	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
830	
831	```json
832	{
833	  "id": "order-flow",
834	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
835	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
836	}
837	```
838	
839	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
840	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
841	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
842	
843	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
844	
845	```json
846	{
847	  "id": "nightly-orders",
848	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
849	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
850	}
851	```
852	
853	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
854	
855	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
856	
857	```json
858	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
859	```
860	
861	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
862	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
863	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
864	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
865	`false`.
866	
867	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
868	
869	```json
870	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
871	```
872	
873	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
874	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
875	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
876	dependencies of its successors.
877	
878	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
879	
880	```json
881	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
882	```
883	
884	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
885	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
886	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
887	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
888	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
889	`retries_exhausted`.
890	
891	A task may instead declare an approval point:
892	
893	```json
894	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
895	```
896	
897	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
898	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
899	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
900	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
901	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
902	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
903	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
904	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
905	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
906	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
907	move the task.
908	
909	### Submit an approval decision
910	
911	```http
912	POST /executions/run-1/decision
913	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
914	
915	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
916	```
917	
918	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
919	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
920	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
921	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
922	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
923	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
924	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
925	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
926	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
927	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
928	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
929	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
930	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
931	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
932	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
933	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
934	404.
935	
936	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
937	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
938	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
939	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
940	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
941	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
942	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
943	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
944	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
945	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
946	shape and event stream.
947	
948	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
949	segment:
950	
951	```json
952	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
953	```
954	
955	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
956	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
957	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
958	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
959	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
960	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
961	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
962	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
963	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
964	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
965	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
966	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
967	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
968	loop node instead).
969	
970	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
971	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
972	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
973	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
974	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
975	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
976	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
977	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
978	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
979	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
980	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
981	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
982	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
983	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
984	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
985	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
986	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
987	belong only to their iterations.
988	
989	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
990	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
991	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
992	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
993	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
994	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
995	exactly.
996	
997	### Dynamic map nodes
998	
999	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
1000	recorded array:
1001	
1002	```json
1003	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
1004	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
1005	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
1006	```
1007	
1008	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
1009	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
1010	
1011	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
1012	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
1013	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
1014	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
1015	  the same path syntax as a condition.
1016	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
1017	  expand.
1018	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
1019	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
1020	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
1021	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
1022	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
1023	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
1024	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
1025	
1026	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
1027	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
1028	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
1029	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
1030	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
1031	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
1032	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
1033	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
1034	overwrite another instance.
1035	
1036	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
1037	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
1038	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
1039	become available in the usual way.
1040	
1041	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
1042	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
1043	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
1044	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
1045	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
1046	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
1047	
1048	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
1049	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
1050	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
1051	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
1052	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
1053	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
1054	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
1055	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
1056	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
1057	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
1058	
1059	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
1060	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
1061	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
1062	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
1063	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
1064	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
1065	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
1066	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
1067	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
1068	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
1069	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
1070	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
1071	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
1072	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
1073	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
1074	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
1075	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
1076	
1077	### Maps inside loop bodies
1078	
1079	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
1080	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
1081	other body member:
1082	
1083	```json
1084	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
1085	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
1086	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
1087	```
1088	
1089	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
1090	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
1091	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
1092	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
1093	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
1094	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
1095	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
1096	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
1097	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
1098	
1099	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
1100	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
1101	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
1102	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
1103	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
1104	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
1105	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
1106	influence from the iteration number.
1107	
1108	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
1109	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
1110	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
1111	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
1112	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
1113	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
1114	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
1115	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
1116	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
1117	
1118	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
1119	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
1120	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
1121	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
1122	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
1123	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
1124	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
1125	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
1126	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
1127	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
1128	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
1129	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
1130	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
1131	
1132	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
1133	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
1134	
1135	### Delete and modify expanded instances
1136	
1137	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
1138	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
1139	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
1140	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
1141	
1142	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
1143	that has permanently failed:
1144	
1145	```http
1146	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
1147	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
1148	
1149	{}
1150	```
1151	
1152	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
1153	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
1154	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
1155	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
1156	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
1157	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
1158	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
1159	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
1160	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
1161	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
1162	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
1163	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
1164	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
1165	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
1166	
1167	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
1168	before it is worked:
1169	
1170	```http
1171	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
1172	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
1173	
1174	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
1175	```
1176	
1177	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
1178	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
1179	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
1180	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
1181	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
1182	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
1183	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
1184	is stored verbatim.
1185	
1186	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
1187	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
1188	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
1189	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
1190	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
1191	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
1192	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
1193	
1194	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
1195	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
1196	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
1197	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
1198	carries no loop context.
1199	
1200	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
1201	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
1202	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
1203	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
1204	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
1205	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
1206	first result and appends no second event.
1207	
1208	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
1209	
1210	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
1211	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
1212	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
1213	  and `iteration`;
1214	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
1215	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
1216	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
1217	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
1218	
1219	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
1220	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
1221	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
1222	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
1223	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
1224	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
1225	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
1226	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
1227	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
1228	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
1229	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
1230	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
1231	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
1232	
1233	### Re-expand a dynamic node
1234	
1235	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
1236	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
1237	
1238	```http
1239	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
1240	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
1241	
1242	{}
1243	```
1244	
1245	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
1246	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
1247	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
1248	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
1249	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
1250	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
1251	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
1252	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
1253	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
1254	bounds start from zero.
1255	
1256	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
1257	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
1258	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
1259	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
1260	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
1261	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
1262	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
1263	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
1264	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
1265	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
1266	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
1267	expansion.
1268	
1269	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
1270	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
1271	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
1272	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
1273	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
1274	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
1275	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
1276	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
1277	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1278	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
1279	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
1280	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
1281	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
1282	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
1283	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
1284	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
1285	an instance that stayed deleted.
1286	
1287	### Workflow versions
1288	
1289	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
1290	
1291	```json
1292	{
1293	  "id": "order-flow",
1294	  "version": "2026-09-25",
1295	  "nodes": [
1296	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
1297	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
1298	  ]
1299	}
1300	```
1301	
1302	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
1303	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
1304	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
1305	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
1306	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
1307	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
1308	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
1309	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
1310	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
1311	
1312	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
1313	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
1314	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
1315	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
1316	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
1317	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
1318	
1319	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
1320	current version at the moment it starts:
1321	
1322	```http
1323	POST /executions
1324	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
1325	
1326	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
1327	```
1328	
1329	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
1330	
1331	```json
1332	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
1333	```
1334	
1335	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
1336	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
1337	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
1338	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
1339	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
1340	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
1341	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
1342	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
1343	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
1344	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
1345	conclusions never change.
1346	
1347	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
1348	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
1349	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
1350	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1351	stream with no added field.
1352	
1353	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
1354	
1355	```http
1356	GET /workflows/order-flow
1357	```
1358	
1359	```json
1360	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
1361	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
1362	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
1363	]}
1364	```
1365	
1366	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
1367	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
1368	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
1369	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
1370	resources as usual.
1371	
1372	### Migrate a running execution to another version
1373	
1374	```http
